corpus_note: Curated practical dairy-management guidance for the isolated Assistant. Items are general education and triage aids only; they do not read DairyOS farm records and do not prescribe drugs, doses, vaccine schedules or ration formulae.

items.title: Calf colostrum, hydration and scours triage
items.question: How should calf colostrum and scours risk be managed?
items.answer: Treat a calf problem as urgent when the calf is weak, cold, not nursing, dehydrated, has blood in manure, or is worsening. Record the observation, protect hydration and warmth, isolate when infectious disease is possible, and contact the veterinarian promptly.
items.explanation: Good calf care starts with fast, clean colostrum delivery, dry bedding, clean feeding equipment and close observation. Scours is not one disease; it can involve nutrition, hygiene, viruses, bacteria or parasites, so DairyOS should help organise observations and follow-up rather than guess the cause. The useful record is practical: calf identity, age, attitude, suckle reflex, manure description, temperature if measured, hydration signs, treatment already authorised, and whether other calves are affected.

scenario.given: A fictional calf EX-CALF-001 is dull and has watery manure.
steps: Move the calf to a clean, dry and observable space if safe.
Record identity, age, signs, manure appearance and hydration concerns.
Check whether other calves have similar signs.
Escalate to the veterinarian, especially if the calf is weak, bloody, cold or not drinking.
scenario.expected: The farm has a clear triage record and no one treats the Assistant as a diagnosis.
scenario.next: Record the veterinarian-authorised plan and follow-up outcome.

persisted: health observation or case if recorded in DairyOS

sources: MSD Veterinary Manual: Management of neonatal calves

items.clinical_safety: This is triage guidance only. It does not diagnose scours and does not recommend a medicine, electrolyte plan or dose.
items.applicability: General dairy calf-management education; farm protocols, local disease risk and veterinary direction override it.

exceptions.condition: The calf is unable to stand, very cold, bloated, has blood in manure, or will not suck.

items.correction_path: If a calf observation was recorded incorrectly in DairyOS, correct the health record through the governed health workflow rather than deleting evidence.
items.safety: Do not use the Assistant to choose antibiotics, anti-inflammatory drugs or electrolyte dosing.

perspectives.operator: Write down exactly what you see and get help early for weak calves.
perspectives.supervisor: Several calves with similar signs is a herd-level hygiene or infectious-risk signal.
perspectives.finance: Calf disease affects replacement cost and future herd structure.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Clinical diagnosis and treatment plan belong to the veterinarian.
perspectives.technical: The Assistant gives general triage wording and never reads calf records.
perspectives.training: Practice describing signs without naming a diagnosis.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If cases repeat, review colostrum hygiene, bedding, feeding equipment and grouping.

items.title: Dry and close-up cow transition triage
items.question: What should I watch in dry and close-up cows?
items.answer: Watch dry and close-up cows for appetite drop, isolation, abnormal manure, udder changes, lameness, calving difficulty, fever, retained placenta signs and low energy after calving. Record the observation and escalate abnormal or worsening signs.
items.explanation: The transition period is high risk because feed intake, calving stress, udder health and metabolic pressure all change together. DairyOS can help by keeping the lifecycle stage, breeding event, health observation and follow-up evidence linked, but it must not infer a diagnosis from one sign. A practical review looks for pattern and timing: which group, how many cows, relation to calving, feed changes, heat stress and whether milk or rumination has changed.

scenario.given: Fictional cow EX-COW-011 is close-up and stops eating normally.
steps: Confirm lifecycle stage and expected calving context.
Record appetite, attitude, manure, mobility and any calving signs.
Check whether other close-up cows show similar changes.
Escalate promptly when signs are abnormal or worsening.
scenario.expected: The concern is captured as a practical transition-cow risk record, not as an invented diagnosis.
scenario.next: Record the authorised clinical plan and follow-up.

persisted: health observation or case if recorded

sources: MSD Veterinary Manual: Periparturient cow health overview
Veterinarian review required for farm-specific protocols
items.clinical_safety: This item is not a diagnosis and does not prescribe treatment for milk fever, ketosis, metritis or other transition diseases.
items.applicability: General transition-cow monitoring; local veterinary protocols override it.

exceptions.condition: Calving difficulty, down cow, severe depression, fever or foul discharge is suspected.

items.correction_path: Correct the underlying lifecycle, breeding or health record through the owning workflow.
items.safety: Do not delay veterinary care while collecting software evidence.

perspectives.operator: Report appetite and attitude changes early.
perspectives.supervisor: Look for group-level patterns around feed, housing and calving pressure.
perspectives.finance: Transition disease affects milk, fertility, labour and treatment cost.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Use the record to support examination, not replace it.
perspectives.technical: The Assistant explains the triage pattern and does not inspect current cow lists.
perspectives.training: Walk the close-up group and describe signs objectively.
perspectives.troubleshooting: Repeated fresh-cow problems often point to a transition-management issue, not isolated bad luck.

items.title: TMR intake and ration-change triage
items.question: How should I think about TMR intake and ration changes?
items.answer: When intake drops or refusals change, check the basics first: delivered amount, ingredient availability, mixing consistency, water access, heat stress, bunk space, sorting, spoiled feed and whether the right group received the right ration.
items.explanation: DairyOS calculates feed cost and cost of production from recorded ration, herd and finance facts; it does not prove the ration was biologically suitable. Practical nutrition triage begins with what was actually delivered and eaten, then checks whether the management environment changed. A ration formulation decision belongs to the nutritionist or veterinarian, while DairyOS helps preserve the evidence: date, group, ration, ingredients, delivery, leftovers, price authority and milk response.

scenario.given: The milking group leaves unusual refusals after a ration change.
steps: Confirm the ration and group recorded for the day.
Check delivered kilograms, leftovers, missing ingredients and mixing consistency.
Look for heat stress, water or bunk-space constraints.
Escalate formulation concerns to the nutrition adviser.
scenario.expected: The farm can distinguish a recording problem, delivery problem and nutrition-advice problem.
scenario.next: Review milk, feed cost and health observations after the correction.

persisted: feed/TMR entries when recorded in DairyOS

sources: University extension dairy nutrition and TMR management guidance
Nutritionist review required for ration formulation
items.clinical_safety: This is management triage only. It does not formulate a ration, diagnose acidosis, or prescribe minerals or additives.
items.applicability: General dairy nutrition operations; nutritionist and veterinarian advice override it.

exceptions.condition: Several cows are off feed, ill, bloated or showing severe digestive signs.
exceptions.behaviour: Escalate urgently to the veterinarian or nutrition adviser.

items.correction_path: Correct the TMR or Finance record through the owning DairyOS workflow when the recorded fact is wrong.
items.safety: Do not use the Assistant as a ration-formulation engine.

perspectives.operator: Check what was mixed, delivered and left over before guessing.
perspectives.supervisor: A feed issue is often a process issue: ingredient, mixer, water, heat or grouping.
perspectives.finance: Wrong feed facts distort Feed/L, OPEX/L and COP/L.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Sudden intake changes can be a health signal.
perspectives.technical: DairyOS cost calculations need recorded facts, not inferred intake.
perspectives.training: Trace one ration day from ingredients to leftovers to milk response.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If cost changed but ration did not, inspect price authority and herd counts.

items.title: Milk quality and mastitis-pattern triage
items.question: What should I check when milk quality worsens?
items.answer: When milk quality worsens, separate the immediate milk-safety decision from the root-cause review. Hold abnormal or withdrawal milk out of sale, record the animal and signs, then review hygiene, equipment, milking routine, bedding, affected animals and timing.
items.explanation: Milk quality problems can arise from individual udder disease, milking routine, equipment, housing, heat stress, dirty teats, delayed cooling or residue risk. DairyOS should preserve the evidence trail: production date, session, animal identity, disposition, treatment and withdrawal status. It should not declare a mastitis pathogen or milk-sale eligibility from incomplete facts.

scenario.given: The bulk tank result worsens and two fictional cows have abnormal milk.
steps: Keep abnormal or withdrawal milk out of sale.
Record animal identity, session, signs and disposition.
Check whether the pattern is individual, group, equipment or routine related.
Escalate testing and treatment decisions to the veterinarian.
scenario.expected: Milk safety is protected while the evidence needed for root-cause review is retained.
scenario.next: Review repeated patterns by cow, group, session and milking routine.

persisted: milk records, dispositions, health observations and treatments where recorded

sources: Veterinarian and milk buyer rules for farm-specific decisions
items.clinical_safety: This is milk-quality triage only. It does not diagnose mastitis, identify pathogens, set withholding intervals or approve milk for sale; those decisions require the veterinarian or milk-quality authority.
items.applicability: General dairy milk-quality management; local milk-buyer rules and veterinary direction override it.

exceptions.condition: A cow is systemically ill, milk is abnormal, or residue risk exists.
exceptions.behaviour: Hold affected milk out of sale and escalate to the veterinarian or milk-quality authority.

items.correction_path: Use DairyOS milk amendment, disposition and treatment workflows to correct recorded facts.
items.safety: Never use the Assistant to clear milk for sale when treatment, abnormal milk or residue risk is present.

perspectives.operator: Protect the tank first, then record what happened.
perspectives.supervisor: Patterns across cows or sessions often point to routine or equipment.
perspectives.finance: Wastage and withheld milk affect revenue and COP/L.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Culture, diagnosis and treatment belong to clinical authority.
perspectives.technical: Milk quality answers are general knowledge and do not read quality samples.
perspectives.training: Follow one abnormal-milk event through disposition and health records.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If milk totals reconcile but saleable litres fall, inspect dispositions and withdrawal records.

items.title: Welfare triage for heat stress, lameness and comfort
items.question: What welfare signs should I act on quickly?
items.answer: Act quickly on open-mouth breathing, severe heat stress, down cows, severe lameness, injuries, animals unable to reach feed or water, and any worsening pain or distress. Record the observation and escalate urgent cases.
items.explanation: Welfare observations are useful because they capture what the operator saw before it disappears into a general impression. Heat stress, lameness and comfort problems affect milk, fertility, feed intake and health, but the first duty is animal care. DairyOS can organise observations by animal, group, domain and severity; it should not replace stockmanship or clinical judgement.

scenario.given: Several cows in a fictional milking group are panting and one is lame.
steps: Check water, shade, ventilation and access to feed.
Separate urgent individual cases from group-level risk.
Record objective observations and severity.
Escalate pain, severe heat stress or inability to walk.
scenario.expected: Animal welfare is acted on first and DairyOS retains the observation trail.
scenario.next: Review milk, reproduction and health patterns after the welfare event.

persisted: welfare or health observation when recorded

sources: World Organisation for Animal Health welfare principles

items.applicability: General dairy welfare observation guidance; local welfare law and veterinary direction override it.

exceptions.condition: An animal is down, severely lame, injured, in severe heat distress or cannot reach feed or water.
exceptions.behaviour: Escalate urgently and prioritise immediate animal care.

items.correction_path: Correct the source welfare or health observation through the governed workflow.
items.safety: Do not wait for software confirmation before addressing obvious animal distress.

perspectives.operator: Record what you see, but act first when welfare is urgent.
perspectives.supervisor: Group-level welfare signs often reflect facilities or routine.
perspectives.finance: Welfare problems affect production, fertility and treatment cost.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Pain, lameness and severe heat stress may require clinical care.
perspectives.technical: The Assistant explains triage and does not read welfare records.
perspectives.training: Practice scoring observations objectively rather than emotionally.
perspectives.troubleshooting: Repeated alerts suggest a management or facility cause.

items.title: Daily whole-farm review
items.question: What should a daily dairy farm review include?
alternatives: what should I check every day
items.answer: A useful daily review checks herd count changes, milk completeness, abnormal milk and dispositions, feed delivery and refusals, health and welfare attention, breeding events, semen movements, finance entries and unresolved operational findings.
items.explanation: The point of a daily review is not to admire a dashboard; it is to reconcile the farm's major authorities before decisions depend on them. DairyOS can support that by keeping each number traceable to its owning workflow. When a number looks wrong, the answer is not to adjust the summary; it is to inspect the source record and either correct it through the owning workflow or record the missing fact.

scenario.given: A manager starts the morning review on a fictional dairy.
steps: Confirm animal movements and lifecycle changes.
Check milk session completeness and dispositions.
Review TMR delivery, refusals, feed cost and inventory exceptions.
Review health, welfare, vaccination and breeding follow-ups.
Check Finance entries and unresolved operational findings.
scenario.expected: The manager leaves with a short list of source records to fix or decisions to make.
scenario.next: Assign follow-up work and recheck the affected source views.

persisted: nothing by itself; the review points to source workflows

sources: DairyOS authority model and reporting workflow
items.clinical_safety: This item is not clinical advice. Health and welfare concerns discovered during review must follow veterinary and welfare escalation rules.
items.applicability: General dairy management education; each farm can adapt the review order.

exceptions.condition: A dashboard figure disagrees with a source record.
exceptions.behaviour: Treat the source record as authority and investigate the projection.

items.correction_path: Correct the owning source workflow rather than editing an aggregate or report.
items.safety: Do not treat a clean dashboard as proof that animals, milk, feed or finances are complete.

perspectives.operator: Use the review to find missing records and urgent follow-up.
perspectives.supervisor: Assign responsibility for each unresolved item.
perspectives.finance: A daily review protects COP/L and cash reporting from stale inputs.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Clinical concerns found in review need clinical authority.
perspectives.technical: This is a cross-domain checklist, not a database query.
perspectives.training: Run the review on a fictional day and trace each number to its source.
perspectives.troubleshooting: When two surfaces disagree, inspect authority ownership before changing data.
